article.title: Move-Away Case
article.author: Tiqua Jackson
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. A non-relocating parent has legal rights that may allow them to challenge a child's proposed move, request a custody hearing, and seek changes to an existing parenting arrangement. When one parent plans to move to another city or state with the child, the other parent does not necessarily lose their say in the decision. Courts often evaluate relocation disputes using the best interests of the child standard , considering how the move could affect the child's well-being. A move-away lawyer can help the non-relocating parent understand their legal options and take appropriate steps to protect their parental rights. Understanding the available legal protections can help a non-relocating parent respond before the move disrupts an established custody arrangement. The Right to Challenge a Child's Relocation One of the most important rights a non-relocating parent may have is the ability to object to a proposed move. Depending on the state's relocation laws and the existing custody order, the parent may ask the court to restrict the relocation. A parent should review the child custody agreement to determine whether advance notice or court approval is required. A move-away lawyer can explain the applicable requirements and help file an objection when there are valid legal grounds. The Right to Request a Court Hearing When parents cannot agree on relocation, the non-relocating parent may be able to request a court hearing. This allows both parents to present their positions and provide evidence about how the move could affect the child. Courts generally apply the best interests of the child standard when evaluating custody and relocation disputes, although the precise legal test varies by jurisdiction. A judge may consider: The child's relationship with each parent Educational needs Emotional well-being Existing custody arrangements The reasons for the proposed move An experienced move-away lawyer can help organize this evidence and present a clear argument focused on the child's needs rather than solely on the parents' disagreement. The Right to Seek Changes to Custody A proposed relocation may give the non-relocating parent grounds to ask the court to reconsider the current custody arrangement. Depending on state law, the parent may seek primary physical custody or a revised parenting schedule if the move would make the existing arrangement impractical. However, relocation does not automatically mean custody will change. The court will assess the circumstances and apply the relevant legal requirements before deciding whether a modification is appropriate. The Right to Request a Practical Visitation Plan If the court permits the relocation, the non-relocating parent may seek a revised visitation schedule to maintain a meaningful relationship with the child. This could include extended visits during school holidays, alternating holidays, transportation arrangements, and regular video calls. The court may consider travel costs, the child's age, school commitments, and each parent's ability to support continued contact. A move-away lawyer can help negotiate a realistic plan or ask the court to establish clear terms if the parents cannot reach an agreement. Legal Protections Under State Law Relocation rules vary across the United States. For example, California Family Code § 7501 addresses a custodial parent's ability to change a child's residence, subject to the court's authority to restrict a move that would prejudice the child's rights or welfare. The application of this law depends on the custody arrangement and the circumstances of the case. Key Points to Remember A non-relocating parent may challenge a proposed move under applicable state law. The parent may request a hearing and present evidence supporting their position. Relocation may justify seeking a custody modification, depending on the circumstances. Revised visitation and travel arrangements can help preserve parent-child contact. A move-away lawyer can explain legal options and help protect parental rights throughout the process.
